title: 5 places to visit in Fez: medina landmarks and Jnan Sbil
description: Explore five places in Fez: Bab Bou Jeloud, Al-Attarine, Nejjarine, Chouara and Jnan Sbil. A practical route with advice on museum, terrace and religious access.
intro: For a first visit to Fez, choose five places that introduce different sides of the city: Bab Bou Jeloud, Al-Attarine Madrasa, the Nejjarine Museum, Chouara Tannery and Jnan Sbil Gardens. The selection combines a medina gate, a former school, a trading building converted into a museum, a working craft site and a public garden. The aim is to understand what to look at in each place and how its access arrangements work.

The Medina of Fez has been on UNESCO’s World Heritage List since 1981. Its history involves much more than a collection of façades: the urban fabric brings together religious institutions, homes, skilled trades and places of exchange. Understanding those uses makes the visit more rewarding. A museum ticket does not grant access to a commercial terrace, and being able to visit a madrasa does not mean you can enter a mosque. Plan with those distinctions in mind before walking into Fez el-Bali.

sections.heading: 1. Bab Bou Jeloud: a clear reference for entering the medina
paragraphs: Bab Bou Jeloud makes a useful first reference because the Moroccan National Tourism Office presents it as an entrance to the medina and highlights its blue and jade-green tilework. Look at the overall structure before walking through: the arches and decoration help you recognise the gate when orienting yourself later. Maps and signs may also use the spelling Bab Boujloud. Save both versions alongside your accommodation’s name to avoid confusion when asking for directions.

Once inside, there is no need to take every turn immediately. Choose your next destination and move towards a specific reference, allowing space for people carrying goods or doing their shopping. The gate helps explain the transition from outside into the old city’s street pattern. For photographs, find a position showing the three arches and tilework while keeping the passage clear. The image in this guide dates from 2019; it documents the place without establishing current building works or signage.

sections.heading: 2. Al-Attarine: the architecture of a former school
paragraphs: Al-Attarine Madrasa stands near the souk of the same name and Al Quaraouiyine. The Regional Tourism Council dates its construction to 1323–1325, during the Marinid period. Its interest lies in the combination of mosaics, woodwork, plaster decoration and calligraphy. Begin with an overall view, then choose a detail: the relationship between an arch, wall decoration and screens explains more than a sequence of disconnected close-ups.

Distinguish this former school’s heritage visit from admission to nearby prayer spaces. The regional website lists paid admission and two visiting windows: 08:30–12:00 and 14:30–18:30. The entry has no clear update date, so confirm opening and the applicable charge before going, particularly if your arrangements depend on arriving around midday. Explore only the areas open to visitors. Seeing a staircase or an open door does not establish access to every floor.

sections.heading: 3. Nejjarine Museum: a trading building and the crafts of wood
paragraphs: The Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts occupies a former funduq, a building associated with accommodating travellers and commercial exchange. It is worth looking at the courtyard and galleries before concentrating on the exhibits. Both the regional council and the national tourist office’s brochure identify that change of use. The building helps explain how the medina worked through spaces for receiving people, storing products and organising trade.

The collection description distinguishes domestic, architectural and liturgical uses of wood. Choose one theme and compare the function of the objects with the craft involved, rather than trying to remember every exhibit. The regional website publishes daily opening of 10:00–17:30 and paid admission without a numerical price; check the arrangements for your date. If the terrace mentioned in that listing interests you, confirm that it is available. Museum admission, a café stop and a terrace belonging to a different business are separate services.

sections.heading: 4. Chouara: observe the work from an authorised terrace
paragraphs: Chouara is a tannery, a place of production, and that function should shape the visit. The regional council places it near the Fez watercourse and suggests watching the work from neighbouring terraces. From an authorised viewpoint, you can observe the arrangement of the vats and the handling of hides. Activity and colours vary; do not expect to find exactly the scene shown in an archive photograph.

Before going onto a terrace, ask who operates it, whether visitors are allowed and what the conditions are. A view included in a service, a separately charged entrance and a shop-related visit are different arrangements. Agree on any charge before accepting, and keep observing separate from a potential purchase. This guide does not assume free admission to the vats or recommend entering the work area without permission. Ask before photographing people closely and follow local instructions. The documentary image shows workers and vats in 2024 without promising access to the photographer’s position.

sections.heading: 5. Jnan Sbil: a pause among planting and water channels
paragraphs: Jnan Sbil changes the pace after the monuments and trades of the medina. The National Tourism Office describes a public garden with distinct planted spaces; the regional council mentions Andalusian, Mexican and bamboo areas, as well as waterwheels. A visit can focus on walking, taking a break and noticing how the planting relates to channels and other elements of the water system.

There is no need to make this stop depend on finding a fountain running or a pond looking a particular way. The 2023 photograph shows a dry channel, vegetation and a waterwheel in the distance: it is a documentary garden scene rather than a prediction of present conditions. Check which entrance is open and give Jnan Sbil its own block, after leaving the medina or elsewhere in your stay. If you arrive close to closing time, confirm how much visiting time remains before entering.

sections.heading: How to order the walk and prepare your directions
paragraphs: Save an offline map and mark the five full names. One way to organise the visit is to begin at Bab Bou Jeloud, combine Nejjarine and Al-Attarine, continue towards Chouara and leave the gardens for a later block. This groups the visits; it is not turn-by-turn navigation or a route without backtracking. Before setting out, check with your accommodation which entry point you will use and where you can meet transport at the end.

Prioritise the access arrangement that matters most to you. If you want to explore the museum attentively, organise the other stops around its confirmed opening. When hiring a guide, agree on duration, language, included admission and any shopping stops. Do not assume a car can reach the exact door of every medina address. For mobility requirements, ask about the specific route and steps at each building; a list of monuments does not establish accessibility throughout the journey.

sections.heading: Admission, religious respect and a realistic budget
paragraphs: Budget by category: heritage admission, a guide if you choose one, transport, food and any viewpoint or terrace with its own conditions. The Al-Attarine and Nejjarine entries specify paid admission but do not establish one shared price. Check the applicable charge and what each admission includes. When buying crafts, ask about the material and how the object was made, and confirm the total price before deciding.

Madrasas and mosques have different uses and rules. A tourist visit to Al-Attarine does not authorise non-Muslim entry into mosques or restricted prayer spaces. Respect the site boundaries and do not interpret an open door as an invitation to cross them. Official Canadian guidance advises conservative dress and respect for religious and social traditions. For onward travel in Morocco, the guides to Marrakech, Rabat, Tangier and Essaouira offer other cities to compare. Plan their transfers separately rather than treating them as immediate extensions of this walk.

itinerary: Start: recognise Bab Bou Jeloud and check your next destination before entering the medina’s street network. If travelling with others, choose a clear meeting reference and save your accommodation’s contact details. The first section does not need to accumulate turns without a chosen destination.

Heritage block: group Nejjarine and Al-Attarine around their confirmed opening arrangements. Allow an attentive visit to the building that interests you most and a meal break. Al-Attarine’s published split schedule is a reason to check admission before leaving it until midday.

Craft block: continue towards Chouara with an authorised viewpoint and clear conditions. Do not extend the walk by entering working areas that are not open to visitors. Choose your return route or agreed transport afterwards; reaching the tannery does not oblige you to retrace the entire journey on foot.

Gardens: give Jnan Sbil its own time after leaving the medina or at another point in your stay. This lets you adapt the walk to the garden’s actual opening and your energy, rather than turning the fifth stop into a hurried arrival at a closed gate.

faq.question: Which five places should I see on a first visit to Fez?
faq.answer: Bab Bou Jeloud, Al-Attarine Madrasa, the Nejjarine Museum, Chouara Tannery and Jnan Sbil Gardens make a varied selection. The route combines heritage and working crafts with an outdoor break, keeping each place’s admission arrangements distinct.

faq.question: Can I freely enter the working vats at Chouara Tannery?
faq.answer: Do not assume that you can. The regional council recommends observing from nearby terraces. Each viewpoint may have individual conditions, and this guide does not present the production area as a public walking route. Confirm permission, possible charges and access before entering.

faq.question: Does visiting Al-Attarine also allow entry to the mosques of Fez?
faq.answer: No. The madrasa is a heritage visit with its own arrangements. That does not grant non-Muslim visitors entry to mosques or restricted prayer spaces. Follow the instructions for each site and do not cross a boundary because another door or monument allowed admission.

faq.question: What visiting hours are listed for Al-Attarine and Nejjarine?
faq.answer: The regional listings consulted on 12 November 2026 publish daily hours of 08:30–12:00 and 14:30–18:30 for Al-Attarine, and 10:00–17:30 for Nejjarine. They do not show a clear update date, so use them as a reference and confirm opening and admission for your travel date.

faq.question: Are Fez, Fès and Fes different cities?
faq.answer: They are spelling variants for the same Moroccan destination. To help with directions, save individual monument names as well as a precise address or meeting point. Bab Bou Jeloud also appears as Bab Boujloud, a common spelling in tourism sources.

conclusion: These five places introduce Fez through its gates, schools, trading spaces, crafts and gardens. The most useful preparation is knowing what kind of visit you are making at each stop and which access needs confirmation. With those distinctions clear, you can give attention to heritage and everyday work without depending on an unconfirmed entrance, terrace or photographic scene.
